title: Organic forms depart from mathematical ideals only as inanimate forms do

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Organic forms depart from mathematical ideals only as inanimate forms do

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: There is no essential difference between organic and inorganic form: living forms depart from ideal mathematical figures only because secondary forces act alongside the main one, just as no chain hangs as a perfect catenary and no raindrop is a perfect sphere.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: There is no such essential difference between these phenomena of organic form and those which are manifested in portions of inanimate matter. No chain hangs in a perfect catenary and no raindrop is a perfect sphere: and this for the simple reason that forces and resistances other than the main one are inevitably at work.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVII, “On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms”; topic “Mathematics and organic form”. Scope: organic form in general

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch17-01: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.29

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The examples have measurable geometry, but the universal ontological conclusion and unrestricted secondary forces make the account non-falsifiable as stated. Datasets could test narrower ideal-shape models, not this claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Individual organic shapes could be fit by ideal forms plus perturbations, but no finite outcome distinguishes the stated absence of an essential difference from an account allowing organism-specific generative principles.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
“Essential difference” is philosophical.

Any deviation can be assigned post hoc to secondary forces.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The sentence denies an essential difference between organic and inorganic form and explains every departure by unspecified extra forces. Shape archives can measure deviation from a chosen ideal and cannot show that the deviation has the same kind of cause as a sagging chain or an imperfect raindrop. The claim stays conceptual.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The claim says living forms differ from mathematical ideals only in the way inorganic forms do, because secondary forces are always present. Any measured deviation can be assigned to some secondary force, so no dataset result separates the claim from a view that organisms depart from ideals for distinct biological reasons.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: The ideal figure and the secondary forces are chosen after the form is seen.
